description: We’re a team of two Systems Engineers and two Industrial Engineers who love using technology and data to solve real-world problems. Together we bring software development, data analysis, process optimization and project management, taking ideas from concept to working prototype. We’re looking for teammates skilled in UI/UX design, Earth/space science data, or video and storytelling to help us build and pitch a standout solution!
summary:
Cosmic Mail is a free 3D web game for kids aged 8–12 that turns NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars into stories worth remembering. Players become Cosmic Carriers, guided by PIP, a friendly robot companion. They fly the Mailwing to real landing sites: Meridiani Planum, Gusev Crater and Chryse Planitia on Mars, and the Sea of Tranquility and the Ocean of Storms on the Moon. There they find five explorers left behind: Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1, Surveyor 3 and the descent stage of Apollo 11's lunar module, Eagle.

On each site, kids walk the terrain, use a scanner to identify each explorer's key parts, and learn what each one did. Then they seal a letter with the mission's story and send it home to Earth, earning stamps, photos and facts in their Cosmic Album. Completing every delivery unlocks a finale that names the child a Master Carrier, with a certificate and a postcard to keep.

Every part, place and date comes from NASA and JPL sources. Abandoned hardware is often seen as space junk; Cosmic Mail shows it as a record of human curiosity, helping the next generation remember the explorers that came before them. PIP's voice is AI-generated.
details:
What it does and how it works
Cosmic Mail is a free 3D exploration and adventure game that runs in the web browser. Players are Cosmic Carriers working with PIP, a robot companion who has lost part of its memory. From the Mailwing’s cabin they choose a destination on the navigation screen, launch, and pick a landing site from orbit.

On the surface they follow a radar signal to a forgotten explorer and inspect it, and PIP remembers who it was. Then they equip a scanner and aim at three key parts: Opportunity’s camera, Viking 1’s sampling arm, Eagle’s commemorative plaque, and so on. Each scan teaches what that part did.

With every part identified, they seal a letter, watch the explorer’s story, and send it home to Earth. After all five deliveries, a finale lights up the “Cosmic Archive”, writes the child’s name among the stars, and gives them the rank of Master Carrier with a certificate and a postcard to download.

Benefits and intended impact
It turns abandoned hardware, often dismissed as space junk, into a reason to care about exploration history. Kids learn real facts by playing instead of reading: where each explorer landed, when, what it discovered and why it stayed there. The goal is for children aged 8–12 to feel that these machines are part of a story they now help keep alive, and to inspire future explorers.

Tools and technologies

  • TypeScript, React 19 and Vite for the web app.
  • Three.js with React Three Fiber, Drei and post-processing for the 3D worlds.
  • Zustand for game state and progress saved in the browser.
  • Blender for the 3D models of the explorers, the ship and PIP.
  • Kokoro, an open-source text-to-speech model run locally with Python, for PIP’s voice (disclosed as AI-generated).
  • Vitest and Oxlint for automated tests and code quality, plus scripted end-to-end playthroughs in the browser.
  • Remotion and FFmpeg for the demo video.

How it is creative
Instead of a quiz or a slideshow, the story is a postal service across space: every explorer is a “letter” that must reach home. The parts are found by aiming, not by reading lists. The Moon and Mars surfaces are built in code and based on the real landing sites, and Earth can be seen from the Moon. Rewards are meaningful keepsakes rather than points.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every part, place and date comes from official NASA and JPL sources.
  • Age fit: short sentences, a single friendly voice, and no reading-heavy screens.
  • Accessibility: keyboard, mouse and touch controls; an option to scan from a list instead of aiming; reduced motion; a low-graphics mode for slower computers; and subtitles for every line PIP says.
  • Respect for the missions: no official logos or insignia in the generated content.
  • Universal audience: English, not tied to any country.
